title: Given a `List<String>` (for example transaction reference codes), sort them by their length using `Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)`. Show ascending and how to make it descending.
shortTitle: Sort a list of strings by their length using Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)

s1_definition.profdef: `Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)` builds a comparator that orders strings by the `int` returned from `String.length()`, ascending (shortest first), without boxing the length into an `Integer`. Appending `.reversed()` gives longest-first, and `thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())` makes equal-length strings alphabetical.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a mix of reference codes — some short legacy codes, some long new UPI references. Priya wants them sorted from shortest to longest so the old short codes group together. The sort key is simply how many characters each code has.
s1_definition.oneliner: `comparingInt(String::length)` orders strings shortest-to-longest by character count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)` builds a comparator that orders strings by the `int` returned from `String.length()`, ascending (shortest first), without boxing the length into an `Integer`. Appending `.reversed()` gives longest-first, and `thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())` makes equal-length strings alphabetical.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a mix of reference codes — some short legacy codes, some long new UPI references. Priya wants them sorted from shortest to longest so the old short codes group together. The sort key is simply how many characters each code has.

**One line to remember:** `comparingInt(String::length)` orders strings shortest-to-longest by character count.

sections.s2_technical:
`String::length` is a method reference that, for each string, returns its character count as an `int`. `Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)` wraps that into a comparator: given "UPI123" (length 6) and "TX1" (length 3), it returns a positive number so "TX1" sorts first. Using `comparingInt` rather than `comparing` avoids boxing the length into an `Integer`.

To reverse into longest-first, call `.reversed()`. To make the order deterministic when two strings have the same length, append `thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())`, which sorts equal-length strings alphabetically. For example "TX1" and "AB9" are both length 3, and the natural-order tie-break puts "AB9" before "TX1".

This same technique applies to any derived `int` key, such as sorting account numbers by number of digits, or sorting IFSC codes by length. The source list is never mutated because `sorted` produces a new stream.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India migrated from short legacy transaction codes to longer modern references, and a reconciliation report needs them ordered by length so the operations team can visually separate old from new formats. A plain alphabetical sort mixes them up. This is exactly how `comparingInt(String::length)` works — it keys the order on character count.

Problem 2 — Many codes share the same length and the report must be stable. This is exactly how appending a natural-order tie-breaker works — equal-length codes come out alphabetically.

The code defines a `RefCodeService` with `sortByLength`, and a runnable demo over a mix of codes.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: "UPI1234567" (len 10), "TX1" (len 3), "AB9" (len 3), "NEFT00045" (len 9), "IMPS77" (len 6).

Step 1: `comparingInt(String::length)` orders by length ascending: the two length-3 codes first, then 6, then 9, then 10.

Step 2: The natural-order tie-break resolves the two length-3 codes: "AB9" before "TX1".

Step 3: `toList()` returns the new ordered list; the input is unchanged.

```
INFO: Reference codes shortest-first:
INFO:   AB9 (len 3)
INFO:   TX1 (len 3)
INFO:   IMPS77 (len 6)
INFO:   NEFT00045 (len 9)
INFO:   UPI1234567 (len 10)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: ["UPI1234567"/10, "TX1"/3, "AB9"/3, "NEFT00045"/9, "IMPS77"/6]
    │
    ▼
  sorted( comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(naturalOrder()) )
    │
    ├─ by length asc → {3:TX1,AB9}, {6:IMPS77}, {9:NEFT00045}, {10:UPI...}
    └─ tie len 3 → alphabetical → AB9, TX1
    ▼
  toList() → NEW list
    ▼
  Output: AB9, TX1, IMPS77, NEFT00045, UPI1234567
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — RefCodeService ═══

  ┌─ Pattern: comparingInt on derived key (String::length) ──┐
  │ WHY comparingInt: length is int → no Integer boxing.     │
  │ tie-break naturalOrder() for deterministic output.       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        RefCodeService         │
  │  + sortByLength(List<String>) │ comparingInt(length).thenComparing(natural)
  │      : List<String>           │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. sortByLength(codes)
  2.   → sorted(length asc, then alphabetical)
  3.   → toList()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To sort strings by their length I use `Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)`. The method reference `String::length` supplies an int key for each string, and I deliberately use `comparingInt` rather than `comparing` so the length is compared as a primitive int without being boxed into an Integer on every comparison.

By itself that gives shortest-first. To make it longest-first I append `.reversed()`, and to make the result deterministic when several strings share the same length I append `thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())`, which orders equal-length strings alphabetically.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this ordered a reconciliation report of transaction reference codes by length, which let the operations team visually separate the short legacy codes from the longer modern UPI and NEFT references, with equal-length codes coming out alphabetically so the report was stable on every run. The same derived-key technique generalises to anything, like sorting account numbers by digit count, and as always `sorted` returns a new list without mutating the input.
